message.content:
**Earliest historical reference to Jesus Christ (outside the New Testament)**  

| Source | Date (approx.) | What it says | Why it matters |
|--------|----------------|--------------|----------------|
| **Flavius Josephus – *Antiquities of the Jews* (Book 18, Chapter 3)** | 93–94 CE | “...there appeared at that time Jesus, a wise man, if indeed one may call him a man… He was crucified by Pontius Pilate.” | Josephus is a first‑hand Jewish historian writing only a few decades after Jesus’ death. His passage is the earliest surviving non‑Christian testimony that mentions Jesus by name and confirms his execution under Pilate. |
| **Tacitus – *Annals* (Book 15, Chapter 44)** | 116 CE | “The emperor Tiberius, having ordered the execution of the founder of the name ‘Christ’, was…” | Tacitus is a Roman historian. His brief mention confirms that the “Christ” was a real person executed by the Romans, and it corroborates the Christian narrative from an independent Roman perspective. |
| **Pliny the Younger – *Letters* (Letter 3.16)** | 112 CE | “They worship Christ as a god.” | Pliny’s letter to Emperor Trajan records early Christian worship practices, indicating that the cult of Christ was already established in the early 2nd century. |
| **Suetonius – *Lives of the Caesars* (Life of Claudius, Chapter 1)** | 121 CE | “Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome because of disturbances caused by a certain Chrestus.” | Though the passage is ambiguous, many scholars interpret it as a reference to the Christian movement and its leader, “Christ.” |

### Summary

- **Earliest non‑Christian source:** **Josephus** (c. 93–94 CE).  
- **Earliest Roman source:** **Tacitus** (c. 116 CE).  
- **Earliest Christian source:** The Pauline epistles (c. 50–60 CE) and the Gospel of Mark (c. 70 CE).

Thus, the earliest *historical record* that names Jesus Christ is found in Josephus’s *Antiquities of the Jews*, written roughly 30–40 years after Jesus’ death. Subsequent Roman historians confirm his existence and execution, providing independent corroboration of the Christian narrative.
